blocks.prompt: The Panel That Eats Sunlight
blocks.text: A solar panel is made of many little squares. Each square is a solar cell. The cells are made from sand. Sand has silicon in it, and silicon is very good at catching sunlight. When sunlight hits a cell, it knocks tiny bits called electrons loose. The electrons run along a wire. Moving electrons are what we call electricity. One cell makes only a little power. That is why a panel puts many cells side by side. Together they can run a lamp, a fridge, or a whole house. The panel has no moving parts. It just sits still and works.

sand, because sand has silicon in it
electricity

blocks.prompt: How a Panel Catches the Sun
blocks.text: Sunlight is not just light. It is also energy, packed into tiny bundles called photons. Photons leave the sun and cross space in about eight minutes. Some of them land on a solar panel. A panel is a grid of solar cells, and each cell is a thin slice of silicon. Silicon comes from ordinary sand. On its own, silicon is not much use, so makers mix in a trace of other elements. One side of the cell gets a pinch of phosphorus. The other side gets a pinch of boron. That tiny difference builds an invisible electric push inside the cell. When a photon strikes the silicon, it knocks an electron loose. The electric push sends that electron in one direction, out through a wire, through your lights, and back to the panel again. That loop is electricity. Here is the part people get wrong. A solar panel runs on light, not heat. A cold, bright winter day can be better for a panel than a hot, hazy one, because silicon works less well when it gets too warm.

answers: a tiny bundle of light energy

4.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 9 to 10

blocks.prompt: The Accident That Started It
blocks.text: In 1839, a nineteen-year-old French physicist named Edmond Becquerel was experimenting with metal plates in a liquid bath. He noticed something odd. When he shone light on the plates, the needle on his meter moved. Light was making electricity. Nobody, including Becquerel, knew what to do with that. It took more than a century. In 1954, three researchers at Bell Labs in New Jersey, Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller, and Gerald Pearson, built the first silicon solar cell that was actually worth using. It turned about six percent of the sunlight falling on it into electricity. That sounds poor, and it was, but it was roughly six times better than anything before it. The newspapers were thrilled. The cells were also wildly expensive, and for years almost nobody bought them. Then came a customer who did not care about price. In 1958, the United States launched a small satellite called Vanguard 1 with solar cells fixed to its shell. Its battery-powered radio fell silent after about three weeks. Its solar-powered radio kept transmitting for six years. Space had found its power source, and solar cells had found their first real job. Vanguard 1 is still up there. It is the oldest human-made object in orbit, circling quietly, its silicon long since dead.

5.title: The Panel That Eats Sunlight
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: One hour of sunlight on Earth is about a year of world energy
Silicon is the 2nd most common element in the crust
Physics caps a silicon cell near 33 percent
Good panels today reach about 20 to 22 percent
A watt cost about $300 in 1956, under $1 today
Panels are black to waste as little light as possible

blocks.prompt: Why the Cheapest Power in History Took So Long
blocks.text: Every hour, the sun drops more energy onto the Earth than every person on the planet uses in a year. The energy has never been the problem. Catching it has. A solar panel catches sunlight with silicon, the second most common element in the Earth's crust, refined out of ordinary sand. Inside each cell, incoming photons knock electrons loose, and a built-in electric field herds those electrons in one direction, through a wire, and back. That is all a panel does. It has no pistons, no turbines, no moving parts at all. Panels are dark blue or black because they are coated to reflect as little light as possible. Every photon bounced away is a photon wasted. There is a hard ceiling on how well this can work. A silicon cell can only use photons carrying enough energy to knock an electron free. Photons with too little energy pass through and do nothing useful. Photons with too much energy give up the excess as heat. Add up those losses and physics caps an ordinary silicon cell at about thirty-three percent. Today's commercial panels reach roughly twenty to twenty-two percent, which is closer to the ceiling than most people assume. So efficiency was never going to save solar. Price did. In 1956, a watt of solar cell cost around three hundred dollars. Today it costs well under a dollar. The engineer Richard Swanson noticed the pattern: every time the world doubled the total number of panels it had ever built, the price per watt fell by about twenty percent. Factories got better, wafers got thinner, and the industry got enormous. Nobody invented a miracle. They just kept making the same thing, over and over, until it was cheap. One problem remains, and it is not a small one. The sun sets. A panel produces nothing at night and less under cloud, which means the real work of the next twenty years is not catching sunlight. It is storing it.

6.title: The Panel That Eats Sunlight
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Doped with phosphorus on top, boron below
The p-n junction builds a permanent electric field
Silicon's bandgap is about 1.1 electron volts
Shockley and Queisser proved the limit in 1961
One cell makes about half a volt
Opportunity ran on solar for 14 years

blocks.prompt: No Moving Parts: How a Sheet of Sand Beat the Turbine
blocks.text: A solar panel is the strangest power plant ever built, because it is not really a plant at all. A coal station burns fuel to boil water to spin a turbine to turn a magnet inside a coil. Four steps, each one shedding heat, each one wearing out bearings. A solar panel skips all of it. Light goes in one side and current comes out the other, and nothing anywhere inside the panel moves. The trick lives in a slice of silicon about as thick as a few sheets of paper. Pure silicon is a poor conductor. Its electrons are locked into bonds and will not budge. So manufacturers deliberately contaminate it. Into the top layer they diffuse a trace of phosphorus, an atom carrying one more outer electron than silicon needs, which leaves spare electrons rattling around loose. Into the layer below they add boron, which has one fewer, leaving vacancies that behave like positive charges. Where the two layers meet, at what engineers call the p-n junction, electrons drift across, vacancies drift back, and the resulting imbalance builds a permanent electric field along the boundary. That field is the whole invention. It is a one-way street for electrons, and it is already there before the sun comes up. Now add a photon. Silicon has a bandgap of about 1.1 electron volts, which is the entry fee an arriving photon must pay to knock an electron out of its bond. Red light barely covers it. Blue light overpays, and the change is returned as waste heat. Infrared light cannot pay at all and slips through the cell as though it were glass. The electrons that do come free are swept across the junction by that built-in field, pushed out into a wire, through whatever you have plugged in, and back to the other side. A single cell generates only about half a volt, so a panel wires sixty or more of them in a row, like batteries stacked in a flashlight. Understand the bandgap and you understand solar's ceiling. In 1961, William Shockley and Hans Queisser did the arithmetic and proved that a single-junction cell can never convert more than roughly a third of the sunlight striking it, no matter how well it is made. That result was not a challenge to be beaten. It was a law to be planned around. So the industry stopped chasing physics and started chasing manufacturing. Solar cells cost about three hundred dollars per watt in 1956 and now cost under a dollar. Richard Swanson observed that the price fell about twenty percent for every doubling of the panels ever produced, a pattern that has held for decades. The result is that the cheapest electricity now available to human beings, across much of the sunny world, comes from a sheet of doped sand with no moving parts and a twenty-five year warranty. The catch has never been the panel. It is the night. Panels also fail in ways that reveal how simple they are. The Mars rovers Spirit and Opportunity ran on solar arrays, and what finally finished Opportunity, after fourteen years of a mission planned for ninety days, was not a broken part. It was a planet-wide dust storm that blotted out the sun.
